Neurology · published research

Cognitive performance

Small controlled studies report improvements in selected working-memory and attention tasks after transcranial PBM, including a 55-person crossover study. They do not establish sustained improvement in daily cognitive function.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small controlled studies report improvements in selected working-memory and attention tasks after transcranial PBM, including a 55-person crossover study. They do not establish sustained improvement in daily cognitive function.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact cognitive-performance category contains 29 unique titles: 19 human reports, seven animal studies, two reviews and one meta-analysis. The human literature includes 13 randomized reports and six other controlled or non-randomized reports. Many experiments test healthy volunteers during a specific laboratory task, and several reports from the same research groups use similar procedures. Review and meta-analysis records summarize these primary studies rather than adding participant cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

A randomized, sham-controlled crossover study in 55 healthy older adults tested one session of 1064-nm near-infrared laser stimulation over the right prefrontal cortex. Accuracy and reaction time improved on a 3-back working-memory task during the active session, alongside changes in fNIRS measures of brain connectivity (Yang et al. 2025). Other small crossover studies report changes in visual working memory, sentence processing, vigilance or sleepiness after single exposures. Some studies find a physiological change without a matching improvement in behavior, and the tested tasks do not demonstrate better performance in work, study or ordinary daily activities. Meta-analyses pool different populations and outcomes, so their estimates should not be read as evidence for one standardized protocol.

Animal evidence

Seven animal publications examine learning or attention-related outcomes, including memory tasks in rodents. These studies help investigate dose and biological mechanisms but do not establish cognitive enhancement in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Studies use red visible or near-infrared light, including 660, 810, 850 and 1064 nm, with both lasers and LED devices. Applications are usually transcranial and often target the prefrontal cortex. Schedules range from a single exposure to repeated daily sessions over about a week. The 2025 crossover study used one 12-minute 1064-nm laser exposure in each phase with a long washout. Other studies use different power, dose, target area and task timing, which prevents treating their results as one dose-response estimate.

Interpretation

The evidence supports immediate, task-specific effects under some laboratory conditions. It remains uncertain whether these effects replicate across independent groups, persist over time or improve practical functioning. Sample sizes are small, tasks differ and follow-up is generally brief, so the result should be understood as an experimental performance effect rather than a durable cognitive benefit.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow to moderate for immediate performance on specific working-memory, attention or reaction-time tasks in healthy adults. Low for lasting gains in everyday cognitive function.
Publications and records29 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The strongest evidence comes from small randomized crossover and sham-controlled studies, many testing performance during or soon after one session. Results vary by task, dose and wavelength, and long-term daily functioning is rarely measured. Independent trials should prespecify a small set of validated tasks and test whether gains persist outside the laboratory.
